_comment: Round 25 T4 - the blit ratio gate. Each pinned pair names one FAST scenario (a blit emission) and
its SCALAR TWIN: the same shape, same payload, same process, whose element type is declared
[StructLayout(Auto)] so the layout is unprovable and the element loop is emitted instead. Same bytes
moved, different strategy.
WHAT THIS GATE IS. It is a STRUCTURAL check wearing a stopwatch, not a performance measurement. It
answers one question: is the fast path still being emitted at all? A blit that stopped being emitted
collapses its pair to roughly 1.0x and fails here. That is the regression this round can actually
suffer - a proof tightened, a shape dropped from the gate, an emitter refactored - and nothing else
in the suite would notice, because the OUTPUT stays correct either way. That is what makes a silent
performance regression silent.
WHY A RATIO, NEVER AN ABSOLUTE TIME. On a shared runner a 2% absolute gate yields roughly 45% false
positives, and holding a 1% false-positive rate needs about a 7% threshold. A same-process ratio
cancels the contention both arms feel equally. This also keeps faith with the house rule that smoke
TIMINGS are non-gates: no absolute time is asserted here, and the floor is set far below the measured
margin precisely so ShortRun noise cannot reach it.
WHY n=1000 AND NOT LARGER. Measured locally 2026-08-23 (benchmarks/results/2026-08-23-round25-kernels.md):
at n=65536 both arms are memory-bandwidth-bound and the ratio collapses toward 1.0 - array->List
reproduced BELOW 1.0 across two runs. A gate at the large size would fail on green code. The win lives
in-cache, which is also where real DTO collections live.
ONE PAIR PER EMITTER, deliberately: SynthesizeBlit (array->array, which the enum-array blit also uses)
and SynthesizeBlitListShape (array->List, which the List and ImmutableArray shapes also use). Covering
every shape would add runtime without adding reach.
UPDATE PROTOCOL. Same as the allocation baseline: the floor moves only to a value measured in the same
commit, with the reason. Raising it after a real improvement is the normal move. Lowering it demands an
explanation of what got slower and why that is acceptable.

measuredWith.note: measured ratios were 2.35x (array) and 3.31x (list); the floor sits well below both so that ShortRun noise cannot reach it
